title: Preparing for a Mortgage
subtitle: Build the file a lender can assess before you tour the house your budget cannot

blocks.text: A mortgage application is where your dream kitchen meets a folder full of pay stubs and discovers the folder has questions.

This course lets you rehearse the lender’s conversation before it happens. You will organize your credit, income, debt and cash papers, estimate your ratios and learn what the stress test does. Then you will set a buying ceiling that leaves room for life after closing. The goal is being ready, not chasing a preapproval number that makes your budget nervous.
A preapproval is a conditional estimate, not a promised loan. The property, the down payment, your papers and a final review still matter.

blocks.extra: The four files come next, then Rina’s story shows what a ceiling is worth.

sections.title: The Four Files Behind the Application

blocks.text: Build these four files before an offer deadline turns your scanner into a household celebrity.

items.title: CREDIT FILE
items.text: Review both reports for errors, late payments, high card balances and inquiries you do not know. Do not open new credit just to “look stronger.”

items.title: INCOME FILE
items.text: Gather your ID, an employment letter, pay stubs and any statements a lender asks for. If you are self-employed, expect to show two years of CRA notices and proof of the business.

items.title: DEBT FILE
items.text: List the required monthly payment on every card, line, loan, support order and other commitment. Lenders usually use the required payment, not what you choose to pay.

items.title: CASH FILE
items.text: Document your down payment, deposit, closing costs, moving, quick repairs and an emergency reserve. Be ready to explain any large transfer.

blocks.text: FCAC gives 39% as the guideline for housing costs (GDS) and 44% for total debt (TDS). Lenders may set their own policy, and qualifying for a loan is not the same as affording it comfortably.

items.title: GDS
items.text: Housing costs ÷ gross monthly income. Housing costs are the mortgage payment, property taxes, heating and 50% of condo fees.

items.title: TDS
items.text: (Housing costs + other debt payments) ÷ gross income. Add the required payments on cards, lines, loans, support and other commitments.

blocks.text: At federally regulated lenders, the uninsured minimum qualifying rate is the greater of your contract rate + 2 percentage points or 5.25%.

items.title: “A strong credit score can replace missing income or down-payment proof.”
items.text: Credit is one piece. A lender still needs acceptable income, debt, down-payment and property evidence.

blocks.text: FCAC: Preparing for a mortgage
OSFI: Minimum qualifying rate
Meet Rina
paragraphs: Rina Patel is a respiratory therapist in Brampton. She wants a two-bedroom condo near work. She has saved a down payment and paid every bill on time.
Then her preapproval arrives, and it is a surprise. The number is big. It feels like a game-show prize: bright, shiny and a little dangerous to carry home.

She finds a condo near the top of that number. It has a renovated kitchen and “reasonable” fees. The lender counts part of the fee, the taxes and the heat. Rina’s life has to carry the rest: insurance, commuting, repairs, groceries and an emergency reserve. The lender’s math and her life are related. They are not twins.
Rina has a choice. She can bid at the number on the page, or she can work out her own. She picks her own.

She fixes an old address and pays down a card. She gathers her pay, her job letter and her down-payment proof. Then she runs housing at the stress-test rate and adds the costs that do not politely disappear after closing. Her ceiling lands $48,000 below the preapproval.
The first condo fails her test. A special assessment is being discussed, closing would eat her reserve and the monthly cost leaves no room for a renewal. She walks away.
Two months later she finds a smaller unit with cleaner papers, priced under her ceiling. The appraisal and final review still have to happen, and she waits for both.

The preapproval told her what a lender might consider. Her file told her how much home she could carry while sleeping normally. And occasionally she orders dinner without convening a budget committee.

blocks.text: Rina used the preapproval as a boundary, not a target.
What resolved the conflict?
She combined the lender’s evidence with a household stress test, and she let the lower, safer number guide her search.
You can find your own safe number before a lender hands you theirs.
blocks.detail: You will check your cash, from down payment to closing costs to reserve, so one surprise never decides the purchase.

blocks.text: Cash screen

items.title: UP TO $500,000
items.text: 5%. This is the current minimum for an insured down payment.

items.title: $500,000 TO BELOW $1.5M
items.text: 5% of the first $500,000, plus 10% of the amount above it.

items.title: $1.5M OR MORE
items.text: 20% or more. Mortgage loan insurance is not available.

blocks.text: Mortgage loan insurance protects the lender if the borrower defaults. The premium is a borrowing cost. It does not protect the homeowner.
Eligible first-time buyers and buyers of new builds may qualify for an insured amortization of up to 30 years. A longer amortization can lower the payment, but it usually means more total interest.
SAVINGS-PROGRAM CHECKPOINT
An eligible first-time buyer may use both an FHSA and the Home Buyers’ Plan for the same qualifying home.
Current CRA limits include $8,000 of first-year FHSA room, a $40,000 lifetime FHSA limit and a $60,000 HBP withdrawal limit. Eligibility, timing, tax and repayment rules apply.
The down payment is one envelope. Keep separate cash for closing, moving, repairs and an emergency buffer after closing.

items.title: “A 30-year amortization makes the home cheaper.”
items.text: It may lower the scheduled payment, but a longer path can add total interest. Compare the relief with the total cost and the renewal risk.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why can a preapproval change before closing?
items.detail: It is conditional. A change in your finances, missing proof, the property appraisal or lender rules can change the final decision.

items.title: What is the minimum down payment on a $700,000 insured purchase?
items.detail: $45,000. That is 5% of the first $500,000 ($25,000) plus 10% of the remaining $200,000 ($20,000).

items.title: If the contract rate is 4.80%, what uninsured stress-test rate applies?
items.detail: 6.80%. That is the greater of 4.80% + 2 percentage points and 5.25%.

items.title: What goes into GDS, and what does TDS add?
items.detail: GDS counts the mortgage payment, property taxes, heating and 50% of condo fees. TDS adds your other required debt payments.

items.title: What is the trade-off of a longer amortization?
items.detail: A lower scheduled payment can mean more total interest and more risk at renewal.

sections.title: Your Action: Build Your Mortgage-Readiness File

blocks.text: Use verified figures and partial references. This is preparation, not approval, and it is not mortgage, tax or legal advice.
A complete file does not guarantee approval. It cuts avoidable surprises and makes your affordability decision easier to defend.

items.title: Preapproval
items.text: A conditional estimate of the mortgage amount and terms a lender may consider.

items.title: GDS ratio
items.text: Gross debt service. Qualifying housing costs divided by gross household income.

items.title: TDS ratio
items.text: Total debt service. Qualifying housing costs plus other required debt payments, divided by gross income.

items.title: Stress test
items.text: A test of whether you can still pay at a rate above your contract rate.

items.title: Amortization
items.text: The estimated time it takes to repay the mortgage in full at the assumed rate and payment.

items.title: Mortgage loan insurance
items.text: Insurance that protects the lender on an eligible high-ratio mortgage. The borrower usually pays the premium.

What other required debt payments do you have, and what is your estimated TDS?
How much is your down payment, where is it from and how will you show it?
How much cash do you need for closing, moving, repairs and a buffer?
Which documents or explanations are still missing?
What is your personal price ceiling, and when will you review it?
